title: Inference Time Nash Alignment
claim: Sampling-based inference-time alignment approaches fine-tuned model performance as sample count grows, and stays robust across the regularization strength.
layout: 2 side-by-side stacked-bar panels, left-to-right, line overlay with dashed baseline
description: Two side-by-side stacked bar charts share a y-axis of expected rates (%) from 0 to 100. Each bar splits into green Win, gray Draw and red Lose segments, with numeric labels. A dark blue line with circular markers traces the expected win rate (EWR) across bars, and a dashed red horizontal line marks the DPO baseline at 74.5. Panel (a) shows a DPO reference bar followed by bars for N = 2^0 to 2^6 samples in Best-of-Nash. Its EWR rises from 62.9 to about 74 and approaches the DPO line. Panel (b) shows Nash Mirror Descent with N fixed at 64 and beta from 0.125 to 4. Its EWR stays flat near 73 to 74. A legend sits in the lower right of each panel, and captions (a) and (b) sit below.
caption: Win/Draw/Lose distribution and expected win-rate (Win + Draw/2) on the TLDR dataset. The dashed line indicates the baseline score for LLaMA3-DPO. We use LLaMA3-SFT as the reference policy and LLaMA3-PM as the preference oracle bP.
abstract: Preference-based fine-tuning methods such as RLHF and DPO require substantial compute and large preference datasets. They also need direct access to the model parameters which are not provided by many state-of-the art models. Inference-time alignment offers a cost-effective alternative without updating model parameters. However, existing inference-time methods rely on a scalar reward model derived under a Bradley-Terry assumption, which cannot represent general preferences. Following recent work on fine-tuning with generalized preferences, in this work, we initiate the study of inference-time alignment under general preferences. We formulate the problem as obtaining a Nash equilibrium of a two-player zero-sum game between policies. We propose two algorithms: Best-of-Nash (BoN) and Nash Mirror Descent (NMD). We prove that both algorithms achieve a duality gap that matches the problem lower bound. Empirically, we implement the two methods on three datasets, which shows that our methods substantially outperform the base policy, converging to the performance of the fine-tuned models. Moreover, our results show that NMD remains robust across the regularization parameter.
